title: Estimating Limits from Graphs and Tables
short: Read limits from the left and the right.

blocks.html: You can often estimate a limit before you can compute it, from a table of values or from a graph. The key is to approach from both sides separately.

The left-hand limit $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x)$ uses $x < a$; the right-hand limit $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$ uses $x > a$. The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal, and then it is that common value. In a table, read the values as $x$ closes in on $a$ from each side; on a graph, follow the curve toward $x = a$ from each side and note the height it heads for.

$x$ can approach $a$ from two directions. If the values head to $2$ from the left but to $3$ from the right, there is no single number they all get close to, so the two-sided limit does not exist. The dot at $x = a$ itself, if there is one, plays no part.

blocks.name: limit
blocks.cap: A jump at $x = 1$: from the left the values approach $2$, from the right they approach $3$. The two-sided limit does not exist.

head: $x$
blocks.cap: Values of $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ (with $x$ in radians) near $0$, where the function itself is undefined.

blocks.title: From a table
blocks.q: Use the table above to estimate $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}$.
steps: From the left ($-0.1$, $-0.01$, $-0.001$) the values climb toward $1$.
From the right the values match, also approaching $1$.
blocks.a: $1$ (an important limit you will meet again in calculus)

blocks.title: A jump
blocks.q: $f(x) = x + 1$ for $x < 1$ and $f(x) = x + 2$ for $x \ge 1$. Find both one-sided limits at $1$ and the two-sided limit.
blocks.a: $2$, $3$; the two-sided limit does not exist

blocks.title: A hole with a stray dot
blocks.q: A graph follows the line $y = 4 - x$ on both sides of $x = 1$, with an open circle at $(1, 3)$ and a filled dot at $(1, 0)$. Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$ and $f(1)$.
steps: From both sides the curve heads to the open circle at height $3$.
The filled dot says $f(1) = 0$, but that does not affect the limit.

blocks.html: Reading the filled dot instead of where the curve is heading, or checking only one side. Cover the point $x = a$ with your finger and trace toward it from the left, then from the right. If the two traces end at different heights, the limit does not exist.
